evidence_contexts.source_text: Imagine that we are training a language model.
The character *perplexity* of a language model is defined as the inverse of the geometric mean of a set of probabilities, each probability is corresponding to a character in the word.
Hence, we will emphasize language models in this chapter.
Next, we discuss basic concepts of a language model and use this discussion as the inspiration for the design of RNNs.

In practice, it is very common to use natural language processing techniques to process and analyze text (human natural language) data, such as language models in :numref:`sec_language_model` and machine translation models in :numref:`sec_machine_translation`.

For instance, in :numref:`chap_rnn`,
we have relied on RNNs to design language models to generate novella-like text.

For demonstration,
we implemented RNN-based
language models on text data.
The recurrent neural network language models are one example of using a discriminative network (trained to predict the next character) that once trained can act as a generative model.
Synthetic: In philosophy, a person's language model of the world may shape how they speak.

source_payload.proposed_definition_en: a model that estimates or predicts sequences of words or characters in text

evidence_contexts.source_text: ## The Matrix Factorization Model
Matrix Factorization :cite:`Koren.Bell.Volinsky.2009` is a well-established algorithm in the recommender systems literature.
Latent factor models such as matrix factorization are examples of model-based CF.
Although the final score was the result of an ensemble solution (i.e., a combination of many algorithms), the matrix factorization algorithm played a critical role in the final blend.

The first version of matrix factorization model is proposed by Simon Funk in a famous [blog
post](https://sifter.org/~simon/journal/20061211.html) in which he described the idea of factorizing the interaction matrix.
In this section, we will dive into the details of the matrix factorization model and its implementation.
This computation is important in an area called matrix factorization.
# Matrix Factorization
Synthetic: In this chapter, matrix factorization predicts user–item preferences by learning latent factors from an interaction matrix.

source_payload.proposed_definition_en: a latent-factor recommendation model that represents interactions by factorizing an interaction matrix

evidence_contexts.source_text:
Equivalent to :eqref:`eq_additive-attn`,
the query and the key are concatenated
and fed into an MLP with a single hidden layer
whose number of hidden units is $h$, a hyperparameter.

They were proposed based on a very simple insight:
to use an MLP on the channels for each pixel separately :cite:`Lin.Chen.Yan.2013`.

In the last chapter,
we implemented each component of an MLP from scratch
and even showed how to leverage high-level APIs
to roll out the same models effortlessly.

```{.python .input}
# A simple MLP
def get_net():
    net = nn.Sequential()
    net.add(nn.Dense(10, activation='relu'),
            nn.Dense(1))
    net.initialize(init.Xavier())
    return net

# Square loss
loss = gluon.loss.L2Loss()
```

```{.python .input}
#@tab pytorch
# Function for initializing the weights of the network
def init_weights(m):
    if type(m) == nn.Linear:
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(m.weight)

# A simple MLP
def get_net():
    net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 10),
                        nn.ReLU(),
                        nn.Linear(10, 1))
    net.apply(init_weights)
    return net

# Note: `MSELoss` computes squared error without the 1/2 factor
loss = nn.MSELoss(reduction='none')
```

```{.python .input}
#@tab tensorflow
# Vanilla MLP architecture
def get_net():
    net = tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='relu'),
                              tf.keras.layers.Dense(1)])
    return net

# Note: `MeanSquaredError` computes squared error without the 1/2 factor
loss = tf.keras.losses.MeanSquaredError()
```

Now we are ready to [**train the model**].

Because these networks are invariant to the order
of the features,
we could get similar results
regardless of whether we preserve an order 
corresponding to the spatial structure of the pixels
or if we permute the columns of our design matrix
before fitting the MLP's parameters.
For all entries of the reset gate $\mathbf{R}_t$ that are close to 0, the candidate hidden state is the result of an MLP with $\mathbf{X}_t$ as the input.

evidence_contexts.source_text:
The nonvolitional cue is based on
the saliency and conspicuity of objects in the environment.

As shown in :numref:`fig_qkv`,
we can design attention pooling
so that the given query (volitional cue) can interact with keys (nonvolitional cues),
which guides bias selection over values (sensory inputs).

To begin with, consider the simpler case where only
nonvolitional cues are available.

![Using the nonvolitional cue based on saliency (red cup, non-paper), attention is involuntarily directed to the coffee.](../img/eye-coffee.svg)
:width:`400px`
:label:`fig_eye-coffee`

![Attention mechanisms bias selection over values (sensory inputs) via attention pooling, which incorporates queries (volitional cues) and keys (nonvolitional cues).](../img/qkv.svg)
:label:`fig_qkv`

More generally,
every value is paired with a *key*,
which can be thought of the nonvolitional cue of that sensory input.

In this framework,
subjects selectively direct the spotlight of attention
using both the *nonvolitional cue* and *volitional cue*.
* Attention mechanisms bias selection over values (sensory inputs) via attention pooling, which incorporates queries (volitional cues) and keys (nonvolitional cues).
Synthetic: In psychology, a nonvolitional cue can pull attention to a bright object even when the observer intends to look elsewhere.

source_payload.proposed_definition_en: an attention cue arising automatically from salient sensory input rather than deliberate intention
